## SUMMARY^\*
### Criminal Law
In a case in which Todd Mumma was convicted and sentenced for sexual exploitation of a minor in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 2251(a), the panel (1) affirmed the district court’s denial of Mumma’s motion to dismiss the indictment; (2) affirmed the district court’s “personal forfeiture money judgment” in the amount of $160,000, which represented the proceeds from the sale of Mumma’s house where he committed the offense; and (3) vacated the district
Mumma argued that the district court erred in denying his motion to dismiss the indictment. According to Mumma, the indictment provided insufficient notice, because its language was too barebones and failed to allege any specific facts that would establish the elements of the charged offense. The panel rejected this contention because the indictment included the requisite jurisdictional allegation, alleged each of the elements set forth in the statutory text, and contained only the particular statutory alternatives that were relevant to the facts of Mumma’s offense.
The identity of the victim need not be included in the indictment so long as the indictment delineates the elements of the crime, including any elements specifying what was done to the victim. And the indictment was not deficient by failing to describe, with specificity, the manner in which Mumma “employed” or “used” a minor to engage in sexually explicit conduct for purposes of producing a visual depiction. Accordingly, the district court properly denied Mumma’s motion to dismiss the indictment.

deepseek.snippet: A $2,500 arithmetic error kept a restitution issue alive even after the award had been paid and distributed. On October 20, the Ninth Circuit vacated the restitution order in United States v. Mumma and sent it back for recalculation. The government conceded that the total exceeded the sum of its components, but argued that the payment and distribution made the dispute moot. The court identified a remaining consequence: an overpayment finding could support an offset against damages in a pending civil action. That possibility was enough to preserve a live issue, even though the offset was not assured. The panel did not decide whether the government could be ordered to return the money. It also directed clarification of a separate housing-expense calculation and otherwise affirmed the judgment and sentence. For counsel handling parallel proceedings, the lesson is concrete: connect the payment record to the relief still available elsewhere. Reconcile the components, preserve the objection, and explain the remaining consequence rather than assuming that payment ends every appellate issue.

## Background

Todd Mumma lived in Fresno, California, with his then-wife and two stepdaughters. A private investigator turned over a memory card showing his older stepdaughter, M.V., being secretly recorded as she undressed in her bedroom. Agents searched the home in May 2020 and found a hidden camera built into a phone charger in her room. Forensic review showed videos recorded between 2017 and 2019. Mumma had labeled the clips "good" or "great," and he saved dozens of screenshots focused on M.V.'s private areas in a phone application disguised as a calculator.

A grand jury charged Mumma with sexual exploitation of a minor under 18 U.S.C. § 2251(a), with a forfeiture allegation under § 2253. The Government dismissed a second count before trial. The court never asked whether either party wanted the jury to decide the forfeitability of Mumma's house, which he had sold in 2022, and neither side requested it.

The court sentenced Mumma to 252 months in prison, entered a $160,000 personal forfeiture money judgment equal to the house-sale proceeds, and ordered $71,200 in restitution. Todd Mumma lived in Fresno, California, with his then-wife and two stepdaughters. A private investigator turned over a memory card showing his older stepdaughter, M.V., being secretly recorded as she undressed in her bedroom. Agents searched the home in May 2020 and found a hidden camera built into a phone charger in her room. Forensic review showed videos recorded between 2017 and 2019.
A grand jury charged Mumma with sexual exploitation of a minor under 18 U.S.C. § 2251(a), with a forfeiture allegation under § 2253. The Government dismissed a second count before trial. The district court denied his motion to dismiss the indictment for inadequate notice, and a jury convicted him.
The court sentenced Mumma to 252 months in prison, entered a $160,000 personal forfeiture money judgment equal to the house-sale proceeds, and ordered $71,200 in restitution. It declined to order forfeiture tied to his business. Mumma appealed the indictment ruling, the forfeiture, and the restitution calculation.
## The Court’s Holding  
The Ninth Circuit reviewed the indictment de novo and affirmed the denial of the motion to dismiss. The indictment tracked the statute and included the interstate commerce allegation. It pleaded only the alternatives that fit the case: that Mumma employed and used a minor, and that the depiction was produced using materials that had moved in interstate commerce. It also stated the county and an approximately 35-month period. The victim need not be named so long as the elements are set out, and the indictment did not have to describe how Mumma employed or used the minor. The court distinguished a district court decision demanding more detail and disagreed with any suggestion that the word "use" is too vague in a § 2251(a) charge.
On forfeiture, the panel did not decide whether Mumma had a rule-based right to a jury determination of forfeitability of the house, or whether the district court erred by not inquiring. Assuming both, it held any error harmless.

Defendant Todd Mumma appeals his conviction and sentence for sexual exploitation of a minor in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 2251(a) . After a jury found Mumma guilty of this offense, the district court imposed a 252-month prison term and ordered Mumma to pay restitution to the victim, M.V., in the amount of $71,200. The district court also entered a “personal forfeiture money judgment” against Mumma in the amount of $160,000, which represented the proceeds from the sale of Mumma’s house, where he had committed the offense. On appeal, we reject Mumma’s challenge to the adequacy of the indictment, and we further conclude that any error by the district court in failing to ask the parties whether the forfeitability of Mumma’s house should be submitted to the jury was harmless. We conclude, however, that at least one of Mumma’s challenges to the calculation of the restitution award is meritorious, and we therefore vacate the restitution order and remand to the district court to recalculate the amount of restitution in accordance with our instructions. We therefore affirm in part, vacate in part, and remand.
